## **Back to School 2026: Early Childhood Teachers in High-Cost Metros Earn Just $2-$4 Above Minimum Wage**


### **Key takeaways**


-


**Low pay in major metros:** In many high-cost metros, early childhood teachers earn just $2–$4 more than the local minimum wage.


-


**Stiff competition for staff:** Because this pay is comparable to entry-level retail or service work, some early-ed schools are struggling to attract applicants who have easier options in other industries.


-


**Pay transparency is high:** To compete for talent, early childhood programs are increasingly upfront about pay, with 57% of job postings disclosing salary rates, the highest of any educator tier.


-


**The value of certification:** Elementary-high school teachers, who require degrees and licenses, earn a significant premium, making 26-27% more than early childhood educators.


-


**High demand for older grades:** Middle and high school positions account for 40% of all current teaching job openings as the fall season begins.


Heading into the 2026-2027 academic year, ZipRecruiter analyzed active U.S. teaching job listings nationwide, combining compensation and posting data with localized minimum wage policies. Examining pay scales alongside local wage floors highlights where teacher compensation keeps pace with living costs and where early education staffing shortages are most acute.


### **In high-cost cities, early ed teacher salaries pay barely above minimum wage**


Early childhood providers are competing harder than ever for workers. Prospective educators are often weighing two paths: invest in specialized training for a classroom role that pays about the same, or take an entry-level job in retail, customer service, or tipped food service, where the pay is similar, and it’s easier to get hired.


In metro areas with high local wage floors, early childhood education pay hasn’t kept much of a premium over entry-level minimum-wage jobs. There are 17 major metropolitan areas where early childhood educators make less than $5.00 an hour over local minimum wage floors, including Seattle, WA (+$2.11/hr), Jacksonville, FL ($2.31/hr), Orlando, FL ($2.35/hr), Riverside, CA ($2.60/hr), and Sacramento, CA ($4.77/hr).


Nationally, early childhood educators fare better, earning a median of $7.40 more than the national weighted minimum wage ($12.39/hr). While the cushion above the weighted minimum wage is helpful, slow wage growth overall, at 1.5% year-over-year in July, might still be causing these workers to look elsewhere. Though this is a faster pay growth rate than elementary teachers (0.1%) and high school teachers (-0.1%) saw in the past year, as teachers across the board struggle to keep up with[rising classroom costs](https://groundworkcollaborative.org/work/as-students-head-back-to-school-families-face-11-price-hikes/) , a[rising cost of living](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/08/12/cpi-inflation-report-july-2026.html) , and stagnant pay.


### **Despite lower pay, early education jobs lead in salary transparency**


Because early childhood providers may face increased competition from entry-level hourly employers, especially in areas with high minimum wages, pay transparency has become a critical recruitment tool. Early childhood listings lead all teaching tiers in wage disclosure, with 57% of job postings listing explicit salary figures, compared to 42% for elementary and 41% for high school positions. In metros where early childhood teachers make the closest to minimum wage, salary transparency tends to be higher, as these employers are competing for talent.


### **Higher education and state certifications unlock salary benefits**


While early childhood roles struggle with low baseline compensation, educators who invest in a degree and a state teaching license see a clear payoff: the "certification benefit."


-


**Elementary school instruction:** Certified elementary school teacher job postings offer a national median annual salary of $52,000 ($25.00/hr equivalent), a 26% premium over early childhood roles.


-


**Secondary school instruction:** High school and middle school teacher job postings offer a median annual salary of $52,150 ($25.07/hr equivalent), a 27% premium over early childhood teaching roles.


While teachers with the education and certification necessary for these more skilled positions make more than their early childhood education peers, teacher pay is still well below the median salary of all U.S. job postings on ZipRecruiter in July of $65,160.


### **Middle-and high school teachers are usually the most in-demand**


Heading into the fall, among specific K-12 and early education roles, secondary school positions lead overall hiring demand:


-


**Secondary school teachers (middle and high school):** 40% of pre-K and K-12 postings


-


**Early childhood teachers (pre-K and kindergarten):** 34% of pre-K and K-12 postings


-


**Elementary school teachers:** 27% of pre-K and K-12 postings


While high school teacher postings are the largest share, demand for early childhood teachers is rising. In July, months before the seasonal fall peak, job postings were up 13% year-over-year. This doesn’t necessarily indicate an increase in demand for early childhood education workers, as slow wage growth might be pushing some workers towards other industries. In[ZipRecruiter’s Q3 survey of job seekers](https://www.ziprecruiter-research.org/economic-insights-research/job-seeker-confidence-2026-q3) , we found that **87% of job seekers who currently or most recently worked in the education sector are considering jobs in other fields** . Stagnant pay and[stressful workloads](https://www.rand.org/news/press/2026/06/teachers-stress-burnout-continue-to-outpace-those-of.html) certainly have some educators eyeing other opportunities, which could impact the supply of education labor available as another school year kicks off.


### **The year ahead**


As the 2026-27 school year kicks off, local wage dynamics and increasing demand for teachers might make the education job market more competitive for employers. The combination of stagnant wage growth in early childhood roles and high interest among education workers in exploring other fields suggests that recruitment will remain challenging for schools. As providers compete for talent, particularly in high-cost areas where pay is closely tethered to local minimum wage floors, transparency in compensation and the clear salary advantages associated with certification and higher-level roles will likely become even more vital for attracting and retaining educators.


### **Methodology**


Data for this report are sourced from active U.S. job listings on the ZipRecruiter marketplace between January 2022 and July 2026. Teacher positions were defined as instructional classroom roles, excluding non-instructional school support staff such as bus drivers, nurses, and administrators, and were further segmented by grade level and institution type (early childhood, elementary, secondary, and higher education) using job title and description metadata. Salary figures represent the median midpoint of disclosed annual pay ranges, and all trend metrics reflect a 3-month rolling average. Minimum wage data is sourced from the[Economic Policy Institute Minimum Wage Tracker](https://www.epi.org/minimum-wage-tracker/) , taking local, state, and federal minimum wages to create working-population-weighted minimum wages at the metro level.
